title: The desire for God (CCC 27)
hook: the longing for God is written in every heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, the catechism: a map of the faith, not a wall. Your line was four pillars. Believe, celebrate, live, pray. Today we open the first page of the first pillar. Day two hundred ninety-one.

You finally get the thing you wanted. The job, the apartment, the relationship, the trip. And it's good. It really is. But a few weeks later there's a small, familiar feeling, like hunger after a big meal. Is this it? You'd think you were ungrateful. You'd think something was broken in you. Most people have felt that ache, and most keep it to themselves. The Catechism of the Catholic Church doesn't start with rules, or even with God's name. It starts with that ache. Today: the desire for God.
screen: `YOU GET THE THING YOU WANTED.` → `IS THIS IT?` → `THE CATECHISM STARTS WITH THE ACHE.`

segments.voice: First, where it begins. Paragraph 27, the start of the Catechism's first chapter, says the desire for God is written in the human heart, because people are made by God and for God. And it says God never stops drawing people toward himself. Only in God, it says, will a person find the truth and happiness they never stop looking for. So that ache after the good thing isn't a defect. It's a signature. Second, the oldest voice. The Catechism leans on Augustine, who opened his Confessions sixteen centuries ago with a line to God that Catholics still know by heart. In Pusey's translation: "for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." You heard its echo in young Merton's restlessness. Here it becomes the foundation of the whole book. Third, everywhere, always. The Catechism notes that, all through history and across cultures, people have searched for God in prayers, sacrifices, rituals and quiet meditation. It calls the human being a religious being. It doesn't treat that search as a problem, but as a trace of the desire. It also admits honestly that people can forget this longing, or push it away, or never have it named for them. Fourth, the psalm. Long before Augustine, a psalm put it in one picture, in the Douay-Rheims: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God." A deer at a stream, thirsty. Catholics say: that thirst isn't the problem. It's the clue. You were made for more.
screen: `WRITTEN IN THE HUMAN HEART.` · `RESTLESS UNTIL IT REPOSE IN THEE.` · `A RELIGIOUS BEING, EVERYWHERE.` · `THE THIRSTY DEER.` · then, large: `SO MY SOUL PANTETH AFTER THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you long for most. Settle and breathe. Ask yourself, honestly: what do I want? Let the first answers come: money, rest, love, to be understood. Don't judge them. Then ask again, underneath: and what do I want from that? Keep going gently, one layer at a time, until you reach something you can't quite name. Stay there. If you pray, you can offer that longing to God, just as it is. The bell holds the time.
The desire for God. The Catechism's first word about us: a longing written in every human heart, because we're made by God and for God. Today's word.
Your line: made for more. Today, when you feel that little is-this-it ache, don't scold it or scroll it away. Treat it as a clue. Day two hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: The Catechism of the Catholic Church opens its account of the faith with the human desire for God (paragraphs 27–30), and Augustine's line about the restless heart is one of the most quoted sentences in Catholic preaching.

fork.setup: you have the career, the friends, the good life, and you're still restless. what does Augustine say that means?
options: you need a bigger version of the same things
your heart is restless until it rests in God
restlessness is a sin to be ashamed of
fork.reveal: Augustine opens his Confessions saying we were made for God, and the heart is restless until it rests in him. the Catechism builds on it.

original.note: Latin: our heart is restless, from the first chapter of Augustine's Confessions.

trapdoor: what you thought: the desire for God is something only religious people have.
what it means: the Catechism says it's written in every human heart, because we're made by God and for God.
what a scholar hears: CCC 27–30, Augustine's Confessions 1.1 (fecisti nos ad te), the homo religiosus of CCC 28, and Psalm 41 in the Vulgate numbering.
